cards.back: A program learns from experience **E** w.r.t. task **T** and performance measure **P** if its performance at T, measured by P, improves with E. Well-defined task = $\langle P,T,E\rangle$.

cards.front: Role of train / validation / test sets
cards.back: **Train** fits parameters; **validation** tunes & prunes (model selection); **test** is touched once for an unbiased final estimate.
Supervised = labelled data (correct answer). Unsupervised = unlabelled (find structure). Reinforcement = reward/punishment from an environment.
Generative learns the **joint** $p(x,y)$ (can generate). Discriminative learns the **conditional** $p(y\mid x)$ (draws the boundary).
# concepts $= 2^{(\text{feature-space size})}$. # conjunctive hypotheses $= \prod_i (k_i+1) + 1$ (each slot: its values plus '?', +1 for reject-all).
An assumption about the form of the target concept that shrinks the concept space to a searchable hypothesis space. Restriction bias (language) vs Preference bias (search).
The set of all hypotheses in H consistent with the training data. Nesting: Concept ⊇ Hypothesis ⊇ Version.
Start at the most specific hypothesis; for each **positive** example, relax mismatching attributes to '?'. Ignores negatives. No backtracking, no noise handling.
Disjunction of conjunctions: each root→leaf path is an AND of tests, the tree ORs them. More expressive than Find-S.
ID3 → multiway splits, **information gain** (entropy). CART → binary splits, **Gini impurity** (classification) / least squares (regression).
$H(S) = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i$. 0 when pure; max $=1$ for a 50/50 binary split; max $=\log_2 c$ for c classes.
$\text{Gain}(S,A) = H(S) - \sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)$ = expected entropy reduction. ID3 picks the max-gain attribute.
ID3 = **preference** bias from its search (complete space, prefers short trees / Occam). Find-S = **restriction** bias from its space definition (incomplete space).
h overfits if some h′ has higher train error but lower true-distribution error: $\text{err}_{train}(h) < \text{err}_{train}(h')$ yet $\text{err}_D(h) > \text{err}_D(h')$.
Reduced-error: prune whole subtrees if validation accuracy doesn't drop. Rule post-pruning: convert to rules, drop individual preconditions. Post-pruning > pre-pruning.
Sort by the attribute; candidate thresholds = midpoints where the label changes; pick the one with max information gain.
Bias = error from over-simple assumptions (underfit). Variance = sensitivity to the training set (overfit). High variance ⇒ low train err, high test err.
$\text{Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2$. Bias & variance are reducible; $\sigma^2$ (noise) is irreducible.
$h_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta^\top x}} = P(y=1\mid x;\theta)$. Decision boundary at $\theta^\top x = 0$.
$J(\theta) = -\frac{1}{m}\sum [y\log h_\theta(x) + (1-y)\log(1-h_\theta(x))]$. Convex → gradient descent finds the global min.
Eager builds a global model up front (cheap prediction) — e.g. Decision Tree. Lazy stores data, works per query (expensive prediction) — e.g. KNN.
Find k nearest by distance. Classification → mode of neighbours; Regression → mean. Distances: Euclidean (q=2), Manhattan (q=1), Minkowski (general).

cards.front: KNN: choosing k & curse of dimensionality
cards.back: Small k → high variance; large k → high bias. Try $k=\sqrt{n}$ or elbow method. In high d, neighbours fill the space ($\ell\approx(k/n)^{1/d}\to 1$) → 'nearest' loses meaning.
P $=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}$, R $=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$, Spec $=\frac{TN}{TN+FP}$, F1 $=\frac{2PR}{P+R}$ (harmonic mean). Precision↔FP cost; Recall↔FN cost.
ROC plots TPR vs FPR across thresholds. (0,1)=perfect, diagonal=random. AUC: 1=perfect, 0.5=random, 0=inverted. Higher AUC = better separation.
